source_text: His igitur maxime actis in primo libro, quorum unum aliquod abunde sufficit ad victoriam veritatis; ex abundanti quidem, superest tamen, ut Magistri Gentium, qua per unum hominem peccatum dixit intrasse in mundum [n20] , sententiam disputemus; et definitionibus, quas praemisimus, cum necesse fuerit, adiuvandi; et probaturi nihil rationem fuisse mentitam; sed iniustitiae esse crimen, aliorum studia aliorum ortibus imputare; hocque ipsum quod iniquum est, quamvis nemo hinc dubitare debuerit, tamen Deo displicere, et ab eodem prohiberi, testimoniis legis, vel in hoc libro, vel in sequenti docebimus. Ex quibus necessario conficitur, et nos rectissime defendere, neminem cum peccato nasci, et Deum reos non posse iudicare nascentes; ac per hoc, tam integrum esse liberum arbitrium, quam ante voluntatis propriae usum innoxiam in unoquoque naturam.
pass_a_gloss: These things, therefore, having been especially done in the first book, of which any one abundantly suffices for the victory of truth; from abundance indeed, it nevertheless remains that we dispute the sentence of the Teacher of the Gentiles, by which he said that through one human being sin entered into the world; both to be helped, when it shall have been necessary, by the definitions which we have sent ahead; and about to prove that reason has lied in nothing; but that it is a crime of injustice to impute the pursuits of some to the births of others; and this itself which is iniquitous, although no one ought to have doubted from this, nevertheless that it displeases God and is forbidden by the same we will teach by testimonies of the law, either in this book or in the following. From which it is necessarily brought about both that we most rightly defend that no one is born with sin, and that God cannot judge those being born as defendants; and through this, that free decision is as intact as, before the use of one's own will, nature in each one is harmless.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere

pass_b_english: These are the principal points established in the first book. Any one of them alone is amply sufficient for the victory of truth. Although the further work is more than necessary, it remains for us to discuss the Teacher of the Gentiles’ statement that sin entered the world through one man (Romans 5:12). We will use the definitions already given whenever necessary and prove that reason has said nothing false. It is an act of injustice to charge some people’s births with other people’s deliberate deeds. Through testimonies from the law, in this book or the next, we will also show that this very injustice displeases God and is forbidden by him, although no one should have doubted it. These points necessarily establish both that we are entirely right to maintain that no one is born with sin and that God cannot judge newborn children guilty. Free will is therefore as intact as each person’s nature is innocent before the exercise of that person’s own will.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
